questions.prompt: Which part of the ISAM structure remains static during insertions and deletions in this lecture's model?
options: The number of tuples in the file
The non-leaf levels
Every record value
Every overflow page, which can never change
questions.explanation: Updates affect the leaves and overflow pages while the non-leaf structure stays fixed. The stored data can still change.

questions.prompt: What normally happens when inserting into a full primary ISAM leaf?
options: The entire tree is always replaced by a heap
The record is discarded if its key is not unique
An overflow page associated with that leaf is used or created
The root is always split immediately
questions.explanation: ISAM uses overflow pages instead of rebalancing the index structure in the way a B+ tree does.

questions.prompt: Is an ISAM separator necessarily invalid after the data entry with the same value is deleted?
options: Yes, every separator must correspond to a currently existing record
Yes, the entire index must be rebuilt after every deletion
No, because separators are not used during searches
No, the separator can still correctly route a range of keys
questions.explanation: A separator defines a routing boundary. It does not necessarily assert that an entry with exactly that value currently exists in a leaf.

questions.prompt: Why can heavy insertion make ISAM progressively slower?
options: Overflow chains can grow long and may be unsorted
The fanout automatically grows without limit
Every internal node becomes a one-record page
Key comparison can no longer be used at the root
questions.explanation: Overflow chains add I/O after the initial leaf lookup. Static upper levels do not prevent these chains from growing.

questions.prompt: Which workload suits the ISAM advantage described in the lecture?
options: One requiring absolutely no overflow after any update
Relatively static data with few structural updates
Continuously adding many keys to one full leaf
Continuously changing the complete key order
questions.explanation: Few updates limit overflow growth and benefit from stable internal levels. They do not guarantee that overflow will never occur.

topics.title: ISAM VS. BINARY SEARCH / B+ TREES IN PRACTICE

questions.prompt: What is fanout F in this index-tree model?
options: The number of rows matching a query
The number of overflow chains in the entire database
The maximum number of children of an index node
The number of bytes in a key
questions.explanation: Fanout measures branching capacity. Key size can influence it, but is not its definition.

questions.prompt: With N leaf pages, each step narrows the search space by approximately a factor of F. What approximates the number of edges down to a leaf?
options: N·F
N+F
log_N F
log_F N
questions.explanation: Solving N/F^s=1 gives s=log_F N. Multiplying the page count by the fanout does not measure the depth.

questions.prompt: An ideal full tree has F=10 and N=1000 leaf pages. How many edges lead from the root to a leaf?
questions.explanation: Since 10³=1000, the path has three edges. Four would count the levels, including both root and leaf.

questions.prompt: If the root and one internal level are cached, what can a search avoid?
options: The keys matching the query
Disk I/O for those levels
All logical comparisons
The tree's data entries
questions.explanation: Cached pages are still accessed and compared in memory. They simply do not require disk reads for that search.

questions.prompt: Why does high fanout often help a disk-based index compared with binary branching?
options: Leaf pages are no longer needed
Every page contains exactly one key
Fewer levels mean fewer page traversals
Every key automatically becomes unique
questions.explanation: Many children per page reduce tree depth. Fanout does not remove leaves or establish key uniqueness.

topics.title: B+ TREE: MOST WIDELY USED INDEX / EXAMPLE B+ TREE

questions.prompt: What does balanced mean for a B+ tree?
options: Every node contains the same number of entries
All keys are separated by equal numerical intervals
Every page is physically contiguous on disk
Every leaf has the same depth
questions.explanation: Balance concerns leaf depth. It does not require identical occupancy or physically adjacent pages.

questions.prompt: Using the lecture's order convention with d=3, how many entries can a non-root node contain?
options: 3 to 6
2 to 3
6 to 7
1 to 3
questions.explanation: The lecture uses d≤entries≤2d. Other references may define order differently, so the convention must be stated.

questions.prompt: For d=2, what is the maximum fanout of an internal node under this convention?
questions.explanation: An internal node can contain at most 2d keys and 2d+1 child pointers. Four counts keys rather than children.

questions.prompt: Why do B+ tree leaves have next/previous links even when their physical pages are not adjacent?
options: To guarantee that all keys are unique
To keep exactly one record in every leaf
To scan between leaves in key order
To replace every search from the root
questions.explanation: The links preserve a logical sequence for range scans. They do not require physical adjacency.

questions.prompt: A root separator is 20, with keys<20 on the left and keys≥20 on the right. Where does a search for 20 go?
options: Left
Both sides are always required
Stop at the root because the record has already been found
Right
questions.explanation: The separator routes the search. Seeing a key in an internal node does not mean that its data entry has been retrieved.

questions.prompt: What is the first step when inserting an entry into a B+ tree?
options: Find the leaf covering the key's range
Insert the record arbitrarily into an internal root node
Split every node before searching
Always create a new leaf, even if space is available
questions.explanation: The algorithm first locates the appropriate leaf and inserts in sorted order. In the basic model, splitting is needed only if the node overflows.

questions.prompt: For d=2, a leaf contains [2,6,10,14]. Insert 8 and split into leaves with 2 and 3 entries. Which result is valid?
questions.explanation: The leaves must remain globally ordered, and each non-root leaf needs at least d=2 entries. The other options violate ordering or minimum occupancy.

questions.prompt: A leaf splits into [2,6] and [8,10,14]. Which key is copied to the parent under the minimum-right convention?
questions.explanation: The minimum key in the right leaf is 8, and it remains in that leaf after being copied. The value 6 is the maximum on the left.

questions.prompt: An internal node temporarily contains [10,20,30,40,50]. If median 30 is pushed to the parent, which keys remain in the two internal nodes?
questions.explanation: An internal-node split pushes the median out of the two new nodes. A leaf split instead copies a separator while retaining the data entry in a leaf.

questions.prompt: Which event can increase a B+ tree's height?
options: A root split that creates a new root
Every cache miss
Every insertion without a split
Every leaf hit
questions.explanation: A split that propagates through the root can add a level. An ordinary insertion does not change the height.

questions.prompt: What does redistribution during insertion try to achieve?
options: Delete the largest key to make space
Use a sibling's spare space to avoid a split when possible
Double every leaf's capacity
Remove the sorted-key requirement
questions.explanation: Redistribution moves entries between siblings while preserving the tree's invariants. It does not discard data or change page capacity.

questions.prompt: The left leaf is [2,4,6,8], the right leaf is [12,14], and d=2. Insert 10 and move one entry to the right leaf. Which result is valid?
questions.explanation: The correct result preserves ordering and the maximum capacity of four entries per leaf. The other options violate a range boundary or exceed capacity.

questions.prompt: For leaves [2,4,6,8] and [10,12,14], what must the minimum-right separator be?
questions.explanation: The right leaf's minimum changed from 12 to 10. Keeping separator 12 would send a search for 10 to the wrong leaf.

questions.prompt: What trade-off does the lecture identify for redistribution?
options: Additional I/O in exchange for better space utilisation
No cost of any kind
It always reduces height by one level
It always makes the tree unbalanced
questions.explanation: Reading and updating a sibling costs I/O. In return, redistribution can avoid allocating a page and splitting a node.

questions.prompt: Why is a leaf's neighbouring sibling relatively easy to access in the approach described?
options: Leaves do not need parent separators
Leaf links provide a direct access path
Every sibling has identical keys
Every leaf must already be cached
questions.explanation: Leaf links help locate a neighbour. The parent separator must still be adjusted when necessary to keep searches correct.

topics.title: DELETING A DATA ENTRY FROM A B+ TREE

questions.prompt: After deletion, a leaf still has at least d entries. What can the textbook algorithm do?
options: Always reduce the tree's height
Always rebuild the entire index
Finish underflow handling
Always merge the leaf with a sibling
questions.explanation: The minimum occupancy is not violated, so underflow repair is unnecessary. Routing information must nevertheless remain valid.

questions.prompt: A leaf has d−1 entries, and a sibling with the same parent has more than d entries. What is the preferred action?
options: Always delete the parent immediately
Always accept the underflow in the textbook algorithm
Duplicate every remaining key
Borrow from or redistribute with the sibling
questions.explanation: The sibling has a spare entry that it can lend while preserving its own minimum occupancy. Merging is used when borrowing is not possible.

questions.prompt: For d=2, leaves are [5] and [9,12,15]. Borrow the smallest right-hand key into the left leaf. What are the result and minimum-right separator?
questions.explanation: Moving 9 makes 12 the new minimum on the right. The old separator 9 no longer describes the required partition.

questions.prompt: A leaf is underfull and its sibling has exactly d entries. What should be done to maintain the textbook minimum?
options: Add an artificial duplicate entry
Merge them and remove the corresponding separator from the parent
Borrow an entry so that the sibling also becomes underfull
Delete both leaves and all their data
questions.explanation: The sibling has no spare entry to lend. Merging preserves the data and requires updating the parent's pointers and separator.

questions.prompt: After a merge, the root has no keys and only one child. What is the correct action?
options: Keep an empty root with no children
Add an arbitrary separator to the root
Make the child the new root, reducing the height
Delete the child and its data as well
questions.explanation: The redundant root can be removed while preserving the existing subtree. The subtree's data must not be deleted.

topics.title: B+ TREE: DELETIONS / REDEFINE OCCUPANCY INVARIANT

questions.prompt: How can a practical deletion policy described in the lecture differ from the textbook algorithm?
options: Delete the entire tree after every deletion
Require every node to remain exactly 100% full
Disallow every record deletion
Allow nodes below half full and reclaim them only when empty
questions.explanation: Some implementations postpone rebalancing to reduce overhead. They do not enforce the textbook minimum entry count after every deletion.

questions.prompt: Why is an entry-count definition of order less suitable for variable-length keys?
options: The same number of entries can occupy very different numbers of bytes
Strings cannot be compared
Leaves are no longer stored in pages
Every key must be unique
questions.explanation: Page capacity is measured in bytes. Counting entries does not accurately measure fullness when entry sizes vary.

questions.prompt: What alternative physical measure of occupancy does the lecture discuss?
options: The number of times the root has been cached
Bytes used
Only the number of tuples returned by a query
The number of distinct table names
questions.explanation: Byte usage reflects actual page capacity. The other quantities do not measure how much space a node occupies.

questions.prompt: Why can Variant C produce variable-length entries even when keys have fixed lengths?
options: The root automatically increases the page size
Every RID must be an unlimited-length string
RID lists can have different lengths
A key changes its data type on every lookup
questions.explanation: The number of records with a given key determines the number of references in its list. A fixed-size key does not make the whole entry fixed-size.

questions.prompt: A page has a payload capacity of 1000 bytes, of which entries use 480 bytes. Has it reached a byte-based half-full threshold?
options: Yes, because it has more than one entry
Yes, because 480 is close to 500
Byte occupancy cannot be compared with capacity
No, it needs 20 more bytes to reach 500
questions.explanation: Half of the 1000-byte capacity is 500 bytes. Entry count or approximate closeness does not satisfy the stated threshold.

questions.prompt: Which property of sorted keys does prefix compression exploit?
options: Nearby keys often share a prefix
Every key must share the same suffix
Every key always has the same length
Keys no longer need to be distinguishable
questions.explanation: A common prefix can be stored once, while individual suffixes preserve the distinctions between keys.

questions.prompt: The keys cat01, cat02, and cat09 use the shared prefix cat0. What are their suffixes?
options: cat01,cat02,cat09
cat,cat,cat
questions.explanation: Removing exactly cat0 leaves the last character of each key. The suffix 01 would retain a zero already included in the prefix.

questions.prompt: What condition must suffix truncation in an internal node preserve?
options: Every separator must be longer than the original key
Ordering comparisons are no longer needed
The shortened separator must still route every search key correctly
The separator must equal a complete leaf record
questions.explanation: Internal keys support routing and may be shortened. The shortened value must not confuse the key ranges.

questions.prompt: Why can every leaf key not simply be truncated to one character?
options: Every string must contain exactly eight characters
Internal nodes have no keys
Prefix compression requires removing the complete suffix
The data entries may no longer be distinguishable or recoverable
questions.explanation: Leaf data must retain the information needed to distinguish and recover entries. Lossless compression differs from shortening a routing separator.

questions.prompt: What is the longest common prefix of alpine and alps?
options: alp
al
alpi
alpine
questions.explanation: The characters a, l, and p match. The next characters differ: i in alpine and s in alps.
